claims.text: A coherent tungsten-based interlayer in HEA multilayer coatings promotes a transition from diffusion-mediated creep to dislocation-mediated creep.
A tungsten-based interlayer reduces grain-boundary diffusion in HEA multilayers.
A coherent interface can promote dislocation activity and plastic deformation in an HEA.
Typical HEA multilayer coatings have incoherent or semi-coherent interfaces.
HEA multilayers with incoherent or semi-coherent interfaces exhibit predominantly diffusion-mediated creep at high temperature.
A thin tungsten or tungsten-based refractory-HEA interlayer can be engineered to form highly coherent interfaces between adjacent HEA layers.
Diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep can compete at elevated temperature and intermediate-to-high stress.
The proposed tungsten interlayer minimizes lattice mismatch with adjacent HEA layers.
Tungsten has a high melting point.
The tungsten interlayer has sufficiently low diffusivity to act as a barrier to atomic migration.
Suppressing atomic diffusion with the tungsten interlayer shifts creep deformation toward dislocation-controlled creep.
Coherent interfaces provide favorable nucleation sites for dislocations.
The tungsten-interlayer multilayer will have a lower creep strain rate than a multilayer without the interlayer at the same stress and temperature.
The tungsten-interlayer multilayer will develop greater dislocation density at its interfaces than the control multilayer.
HEA multilayers without a tungsten interlayer typically have a higher contribution from diffusion-mediated creep at elevated temperature.
The proposed transition is significant only over a temperature and stress range in which dislocation mobility is activated.
Diffusion may again dominate creep at very high temperatures.
The interlayer must retain interface coherency and structural stability during creep testing for the proposed effect to persist.
